Known as the 'Bandit Queen,' this Indian outlaw-turned-politician was charged in absentia over a 1981 massacre before later serving as a member of parliament — who is she?
Phoolan Devi: Indian bandit and politician (1963–2001)

Nicknamed 'the Flautist' for his love of playing the flute at Dionysian festivals, this Macedonian-Greek king ruled Egypt twice and was a descendant of one of Alexander the Great's generals — who was he?
Ptolemy XII Auletes: Ptolemaic King of Egypt, 80–51 BC.
This Cuban revolutionary succeeded his brother as president in 2008 and served as the country's defense minister for nearly five decades — who is he?
Raúl Castro: President of Cuba from 2008 to 2018.
Abrasive and reactionary, this right-wing populist and economic nationalist served as New Zealand's 31st prime minister from 1975 to 1984 — who was he?
Robert Muldoon: Prime Minister of New Zealand from 1975 to 1984. After a troubled childhood, Muldoon served as a corporal and sergeant in the army in the Second World War.
The second son of Libya's longtime leader, this political figure acted as de facto prime minister and was later acknowledged as his father's heir apparent despite once rejecting the role — who is he?
Saif al-Islam Gaddafi: Libyan political figure (1972–2026)
Twice Austria's chancellor, this politician served as the country's top diplomat from 2013 to 2017 before becoming his party's leader and campaigning to modernize the political system — who is he?
Emulating the medieval chevauchée, this scorched-earth 1864 Civil War campaign cut from Atlanta to the captured port of Savannah. What was it called?
Sherman's March to the Sea: 1864 military campaign of the American Civil War.

Considered erotic poetry unlike other biblical books, this text narrates a passionate dialogue between a woman and her lover, warning the 'daughters of Jerusalem' not to awaken love too soon — what is it?
Song of Songs: Book of the Hebrew Bible and the Christian Old Testament.
A former flight attendant who later became a Royal Thai Armed Forces general and the king's bodyguard, she is the fourth wife and current queen of Thailand — who is she?
An economist educated at Cambridge, he served as Singapore's Deputy Prime Minister and central bank chairman before becoming the country's ninth president in 2023 — who is he?

Tharman Shanmugaratnam: President of Singapore since 2023. Tharman Shanmugaratnam (born 25 February 1957) is a Singaporean politician and economist who has served as the ninth president of Singapore since 2023.
According to Herodotus, this 6th-century BC queen of the Massagetae defeated and killed Cyrus the Great in battle — who was she?
Tomyris: 6th-century BC queen of the Massagetae. Tomyris became a popular subject in European art and literature during the Renaissance.
Often called "Sardar," meaning chief, this Gandhian lawyer became India's first Deputy Prime Minister and Home Minister, steering the country's political integration — who was he?
Hitler called him one of his best field commanders and kept dispatching him to salvage collapsing fronts — which hard-driving German field marshal became famous as a master of defensive warfare?
Nicknamed the "Sailor King" for his Royal Navy youth, he was the last king of the House of Hanover and once spent two decades living with the actress Dorothea Jordan — who was he?
William IV: King of the United Kingdom from 1830 to 1837.
The first woman to hold her position, this French politician has led the National Assembly since June 2022 and briefly served as Minister of the Overseas before that — who is she?
Grand Duchess Maria Vladimirovna of Russia
His famous epithet is actually a pun on his name — "noble" plus "counsel" — and this King of the English took the throne after his half-brother Edward the Martyr was assassinated. Who was he?
Æthelred the Unready: King of England (r. 978–1013; 1014–1016)
Which one below was born first?
Henrietta Swan Leavitt (born 1868) is the earliest of the four. Henrietta Swan Leavitt (July 4, 1868 – December 12, 1921) was an American astronomer.
Which of these people was born first?
Qian Xuesen (born 1911) is the earliest of the four.
Which one below was born first?
Ellen Swallow Richards (born 1842) is the earliest of the four. Richards graduated from Westford Academy (second oldest secondary school in Massachusetts) in 1862.
Which of these four has been around longest?
R (programming language) (founded 1993) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four appeared earliest?
SQL (published 1986) is the earliest of the four.
Pick the physicist from these four.
Laura Bassi is a physicist. Laura Maria Caterina Bassi Veratti (29 October 1711 – 20 February 1778) was an Italian physicist and academic.
Pick the chemist from these four.
Antoine Lavoisier is a chemist. It is generally accepted that Lavoisier's great accomplishments in chemistry stem largely from his changing the science from a qualitative to a quantitative one.
What is the atomic number of Nitrogen?
Nitrogen is a chemical element; it has symbol N and atomic number 7.
In what year was Robert F. Kennedy Jr. born?
Robert F. Kennedy Jr.: A member of the prominent Kennedy family, he is a son of Senator and US attorney general Robert F.
In what year was William Howard Taft born?
William Howard Taft: Taft attended Yale and joined Skull and Bones, of which his father was a founding member.
In what year was Terry Gou born?
Terry Gou: Terry Guo (Chinese: 郭台銘; pinyin: Guō Táimíng; Pe̍h-ōe-jī: Koeh Tâi-bêng; born 18 October 1950) is a Taiwanese billionaire businessman and politician.
In what year did Jerry Buss die?
Jerry Buss: Gerald Hatten Buss (January 27, 1933 – February 18, 2013) was an American businessman, investor, chemist, and philanthropist.
In what year did Fritz Haber die?
Fritz Haber: For this work, Haber has been called one of the most important scientists and industrial chemists in human history.
In what year was Proxima Centauri discovered?
Proxima Centauri is the nearest star to Earth after the Sun, located 4.25 light-years (1.3 parsecs) away in the southern constellation of Centaurus.
In what year was Bromine discovered?
Bromine is a chemical element; it has symbol Br and atomic number 35.

Gabapentin: Pfizer. Gabapentin is a
central nervous system (CNS) depressant and derivative of the inhibitory neurotransmitter, GABA.
Which country is Focke-Wulf Fw 190 from?
Focke-Wulf Fw 190: Germany. Along with its well-known counterpart, the Messerschmitt Bf 109, the Fw 190 became the backbone of the Jagdwaffe (Fighter Force) of the Luftwaffe.
Who is credited with discovering Barium?
Barium: Carl Wilhelm Scheele. Barium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ba and atomic number 56.
Who is credited with discovering Lawrencium?
Lawrencium: Albert Ghiorso. Lawrencium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Lr (formerly Lw) and atomic number 103.
Who is credited with discovering Francium?
Francium: Marguerite Perey. Francium is a chemical element; it has symbol Fr and atomic number 87.

Sometimes called a nerve impulse or 'spike,' this rapid rise and fall of voltage across a cell membrane ripples to neighboring spots and fires in neurons, muscle cells, and even some plant cells. What is it?
Action potential (also known as a nerve impulse or "spike" when in a neuron) is a series of quick changes in voltage across a cell membrane.
These tropical arachnids are nicknamed 'whip-spiders,' yet they spin no silk and carry no venom — their name actually means 'blunt tail.' Which order are they?
Amblypygi is an order of arachnids also known as whip-spiders or tailless whip-scorpions, not to be confused with whip-scorpions or vinegaroons that belong to the related order Uropygi.
Found only on male deer, except reindeer, this branching structure of bone and cartilage falls off and regrows from scratch each year — what is it?
Antler are extensions of an animal's skull found in members of the Cervidae (deer) family.

Driven mainly by elevated LDL cholesterol, this chronic inflammatory disease quietly builds plaque-filled lesions in artery walls until, often by middle age, it can trigger a stroke or heart trouble — what is it?
Atherosclerosis is a pattern of the disease arteriosclerosis, characterized by development of abnormalities called lesions in walls of arteries.
This perennial flowering plant species, native to Eurasia and growing up to four feet tall, includes cultivated varieties used for sugar, its edible root, and its edible leaves — what species is it?
Beta vulgaris (beet) is a species of flowering plant in the subfamily Betoideae of the family Amaranthaceae.
This incurable, always-fatal disease of cattle causes abnormal behavior and trouble walking, with symptoms that may take four to five years to appear after infection — what is this disorder called?
Bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), commonly known as mad cow disease, is an incurable and always fatal neurodegenerative disease of cattle.
Sole living family in the mammalian suborder Tylopoda, which group unites camels with llamas and their South American relatives?
Camelidae is a family of mammals belonging to the ungulate order Artiodactyla (even-toed ungulates) and the only living family in the suborder Tylopoda.
This class of ribbon-like parasitic flatworms sheds egg-packed body segments called proglottids into the environment to infect new hosts — what is this class called (scientific name)?
Cestoda is a class of parasitic worms in the flatworm phylum (Platyhelminthes).
This anatomical term for the hollow between a woman's breasts was coined in its modern sense by a Hollywood censor reviewing the 1943 film starring Jane Russell — what is the term?
Cleavage (breasts) is the narrow depression or hollow between the breasts of a woman.
This group of related RNA viruses causes respiratory illnesses ranging from the mild common cold to deadly diseases like SARS, MERS, and COVID-19 — what's this virus family called?
Coronavirus are a group of related RNA viruses that cause diseases in mammals and birds.
Nicknamed for the material that made up most of its airframe, this British twin-engined combat aircraft of World War II was one of the fastest operational planes of 1941. What aircraft is this?
De Havilland Mosquito was a British twin-engined, multi-role combat aircraft, introduced during the Second World War.
This C-shaped first section of the small intestine connects the stomach to the jejunum and is the body's principal site for absorbing iron — what is it?
Duodenum is the first section of the small intestine in most vertebrates, including mammals, reptiles, and birds.

It's the creation of economic value by spotting and commercializing opportunities — a venture that demands serious initiative and shoulders real risk. What is this process, named from a French word for the risk-taker who runs it?

Entrepreneurship is the creation or extraction of economic value by identifying and commercializing opportunities to deliver products or services, a process that typically requires considerable initiation and bears risk.

This synthetic opioid is 50 to 100 times more potent than morphine and is now notorious in emergency medicine. Initially developed as a pain medication for cancer patients and post-surgical recovery, it works by activating opioid receptors — what is this drug?
Fentanyl is a highly potent synthetic opioid of the piperidine family, used primarily as pain medication.
This Canadian physician and author has written five books exploring how childhood trauma shapes conditions from ADHD to addiction, arguing recovery must address underlying emotional pain — who is he?
Gabor Maté (born January 1944) is a Canadian physician and author.
One of the most widely distributed eagles in the Northern Hemisphere, this raptor is dark brown with lighter plumage on its nape and white markings on immature birds — which bird of prey?
Golden eagle (Aquila chrysaetos) is a bird of prey living in the Northern Hemisphere.
This daisy-family genus native to North America and Mexico includes the common sunflower and the Jerusalem artichoke among its roughly 50 species — which genus?
Helianthus is a genus comprising around 50 species of annual and perennial flowering plants in the daisy family Asteraceae commonly known as sunflowers.
This semi-synthetic opioid, often combined with acetaminophen or ibuprofen, treats severe pain and also suppresses cough — what drug is it?
Hydrocodone is a semi-synthetic opioid used to treat pain and as a cough suppressant.

This sudden bleeding into brain tissue or its ventricles is one of two major stroke categories, alongside the blockage-caused kind, and can trigger headache, one-sided weakness, or sudden speech and vision problems — what's the condition?
Intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH), also known as hemorrhagic stroke, is a sudden bleeding into the tissues of the brain (i.e., the parenchyma), into its ventricles, or both.
This financier's 1999 bestseller on mutual funds became an investment classic after he founded a low-cost investing giant — who is he?

John C. Bogle (May 8, 1929 - January 16, 2019) was an American investor, business magnate and philanthropist who was the founder of The Vanguard Group and is credited with popularizing the index fund.
This Arab dessert layers spun pastry dough with cheese, soaked in a sugar syrup, with its most famous variant hailing from the Palestinian city of Nablus — what is it?
Knafeh is a traditional Arab dessert made with kadayif (spun pastry dough) layered with cheese and soaked in a sweet, sugar-based syrup called attar.

Equal to about 9.46 trillion kilometres, this astronomical distance unit is defined by how far illumination travels through a vacuum in 365.25 days — despite its name, it isn't a measure of time. What is it?
Light-year (ly or lyr), is a unit of length used to express astronomical distances and is equal to exactly 9460730472580.8 km, which is approximately 9.46 trillion kilometres or 5.88 trillion miles.
Which Australian nut-producing tree genus, an important bushfood for Aboriginal peoples, was first commercially cultivated at scale not in its native country but in Hawaii?
Macadamia is a genus of four species of trees in the flowering plant family Proteaceae.
It's the science and practice of diagnosing, treating, and preventing disease — from pharmaceuticals and surgery to splints, psychotherapy, and ionizing radiation. What is this field?
Medicine is the science and practice of caring for patients, managing the diagnosis, prognosis, prevention, treatment and palliation of their injury or disease, while promoting their health.

Attaching to its host tree through a structure called the haustorium to steal water and nutrients, this hemiparasitic plant has one species native to the British Isles and much of Europe — what is it?
Mistletoe is the common name for obligate hemiparasitic plants in the order Santalales.
Known for strong anabolic but weak androgenic effects, this synthetic androgen is marketed as Deca-Durabolin and used to treat muscle-wasting and bone-density conditions — which steroid?
Nandrolone is an endogenous androgen. Nandrolone esters are used in the treatment of anemias, cachexia (muscle wasting syndrome), osteoporosis, breast cancer, and for other indications.
This basic mathematical object is used to count, measure, and label, most commonly represented today through the Hindu-Arabic system of ten symbols — what fundamental concept is it?
Number is a mathematical object used to count, measure, and label. The most basic examples are the natural numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and so forth.
This Austrian striker had a brief, injury-hit loan spell at Inter Milan before becoming a regular at Werder Bremen and later playing for a Serbian club. Who is he?
Pan (genus) consists of two extant species: the bonobo and the chimpanzee.
This mammalian skin secretion comes in two types — a watery kind for cooling and an oilier kind found in the armpits that gains odor from bacteria — what is it?
Perspiration is the fluid secreted by sweat glands in the skin of mammals.
Its common name is shared with an unrelated tropical fruit, but this genus of roughly 200 herbaceous species — also called fleaworts — belongs to the family Plantaginaceae. Which genus?
Plantago is a genus of about 200 species of flowering plants in the family Plantaginaceae, commonly called plantains or fleaworts.
Roaming the interior of western and central North America, this even-toed mammal survived the Pleistocene extinction of its close relatives and evolved to resemble an antelope — which creature is it?
Pronghorn (Antilocapra americana) is a species of artiodactyl (even-toed, hoofed) mammal indigenous to interior western and central North America.
Bitter-tasting and rich in vitamin K, this Mediterranean vegetable with edible buds resembling broccoli is also known as broccoli rabe — what is it?
Rapini (broccoli rabe or raab; RAHB) is a green cruciferous vegetable, with the leaves, buds, and stems all being edible; the buds somewhat resemble broccoli.
Operating under a pseudonym borrowed from The Princess Bride, this American created the first modern darknet marketplace before his 2013 FBI arrest — who is he?
Ross Ulbricht (born March 27, 1984) is an American cybercriminal who created and operated Silk Road, the first modern darknet market, from 2011 until his arrest in 2013.
First described in 1779, which large African raptor stands over four feet tall on stilt-like legs and is grouped in its own family, Sagittariidae?
Secretarybird (Sagittarius serpentarius) is a large bird of prey that is endemic to Africa.
Once placed alone in the genus Uncia before phylogenetics moved it into Panthera, this high-altitude cat ranges across the Tibetan Plateau and Himalayas — what is it?
Snow leopard (Panthera uncia) is a species of large cat in the genus Panthera of the family Felidae.
This muscular, hollow organ in the upper digestive tract handles the gastric phase of digestion, and gives us the medical prefix 'gastric' from its Ancient Greek name — name the organ?
Stomach is a muscular, hollow organ in the upper gastrointestinal tract of humans and many other animals, including several invertebrates.

This chalcogen element, chemically similar to selenium and sulfur, is far more abundant in the universe than on Earth because its hydride escaped into space during our planet's formation — which element?
Tellurium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Te and atomic number 52.
What's the name for hardened, foul-smelling deposits of trapped debris that form in the crevices of the tonsils, sometimes visible as white flecks at the back of the throat?
Tonsil stones are mineralizations of debris within the crevices of the tonsils.

First identified in 1801 by a Spanish-Mexican scientist analyzing a mineral he dubbed 'brown lead,' this hard, silvery-grey transition metal carries atomic number 23 and chemical symbol V — what's the element?
Vanadium is a chemical element; it has symbol V and atomic number 23.
Caused by a mutation in the ATP7B gene, this inherited condition lets copper build up in the liver and brain, leading to tremors, personality changes, and yellowing skin — which condition?
Wilson's disease (also called hepatolenticular degeneration) is a genetic disorder characterized by the excess build-up of copper in the body.
This painful collection of pus built up within body tissue often causes redness, warmth, and swelling, and includes boils and carbuncles as common types — what is it called?
Abscess: Localized collection of pus in body tissue. An abscess is a collection of pus that has built up within the tissue of the body, usually caused by bacterial infection.
This wide-body twinjet shares its wing and much of its structure with the four-engined A340, and it first carried passengers for Air Inter in January 1994 — which aircraft is it?
Native to Europe, Western Asia, and North Africa, this flowering plant lent its name — and originally its root — to a fluffy campfire treat, and is used in herbal medicine — which plant?
Its name comes from Latin words meaning 'to strangle' and 'chest,' and it describes pain caused by reduced blood flow to the heart muscle — what is this condition called?
Angina: Chest discomfort due to disorder of the heart muscles.
Also known as pirarucu or paiche, this native of the Amazon River basin is among the largest freshwater fish on Earth — what species is it?

Related to the tufted and horned members of its family found in the Pacific, this seabird breeds from Iceland to Newfoundland and dives underwater to catch zooplankton, small fish and crabs — which auk is this?
Atlantic puffin: Species of seabird. The Atlantic puffin (Fratercula arctica), also known as the common puffin, is a species of seabird in the auk family.

This facial hair — most common among adult men, though it can also appear in women with a condition called hirsutism — has symbolized everything from wisdom and virility to poor hygiene across different cultures — what is it?
Beard: Hair on the chin, lower face and neck.
Made by combining phenol and acetone, this compound forms 65 to 70 percent of the world's polycarbonate plastics production — which chemical?
Bisphenol A: Chemical used in plastics, xenoestrogen.

Unlike most elements, this one is forged entirely by cosmic-ray spallation and supernovae rather than stellar fusion, and is mined from evaporite minerals like borax, mostly in Turkey — which element?
Boron: Chemical element with atomic number 5 (B)
Encompassing reporting, dashboards, data mining, and analytics, this set of strategies and technologies helps companies turn raw data into strategic decisions — what's it called?
Business intelligence: Strategies for analysis and use of data.
Domesticated in Mexico roughly 6,000 years ago, this nightshade produces berries used in cooking, medicine, and even self-defense sprays — which plant species is it?
Capsicum annuum: Species of flowering plant in the nightshade family.
Originally called 'centigrade' from Latin words for a hundred and steps, this SI temperature scale was renamed in 1948 to honor the Swedish astronomer who proposed it in 1742 — which scale?
Celsius: Unit of measurement for temperature.
Once common as the refrigerant "Freon," these carbon-chlorine-fluorine compounds were phased out under the Montreal Protocol for chewing through the ozone layer — what are they?
Home to jellyfish, corals, and sea anemones, this phylum of aquatic invertebrates is defined by specialized stinging cells used to capture prey — what is it?
Cnidaria: Aquatic animal phylum having cnidocytes.

This physician was convicted of involuntary manslaughter in 2011 after inadvertently overdosing his famous patient with the anesthetic propofol, which he had been improperly using as a sleep aid — who is he?
Conrad Murray: American physician and convicted felon (born 1953)
Encompassing roadrunners, koels, and anis among its roughly 150 species, this widespread bird family favors trees but includes some ground-dwellers — what is it?
Cuckoo: Family of birds. The cuckoo family includes the common or European cuckoo, roadrunners, koels, malkohas, couas, coucals, and anis.
This biological process, powered by rhythmic muscle waves called peristalsis, expels solid waste from the digestive tract through the anus or cloaca — what is it?
Defecation: Expulsion of feces from the digestive tract.
A dentist and gambler who fought alongside lawman Wyatt Earp at the O.K. Corral, his reputation claimed dozens of killings though researchers count just one to three — who was this gunfighter?
Doc Holliday: Gambler, gunfighter, and dentist in the American West (1851–1887)
Dubbed 'the father of immunology,' this English physician created the world's first vaccine using cowpox to fight a disease that once killed up to a fifth of city dwellers — who is he?
Native to French Polynesia but nicknamed 'devil's ivy' for staying green even in the dark, this hardy houseplant has become an invasive nuisance worldwide — what's its scientific name?

Famous for the male's song delivered while hovering 50 to 100 metres above open farmland, this streaked greyish-brown bird has been introduced to Australia, New Zealand, Canada and Hawaii — what is it?
Eurasian skylark: Species of bird. The Eurasian skylark (Alauda arvensis), commonly referred to in Europe as the lark, is a passerine bird in the lark family, Alaudidae.
Likely domesticated from the European polecat, with which it can still interbreed to produce hybrids, this slender mustelid averages about 50 centimeters long — what is it?
With atomic number 87 and a most stable isotope whose half-life is just 22 minutes, this alkali metal is the second-rarest naturally occurring element on Earth — which one?
Francium: Chemical element with atomic number 87 (Fr)

Published by Einstein in 1916 as a refinement of Newton's law of gravitation, this geometric framework describes gravity as curved spacetime, summed up by Wheeler as 'space-time tells matter how to move; matter tells space-time how to curve'?
General relativity: Theory of gravitation as curved spacetime. The relation is specified by the Einstein field equations, a system of second-order partial differential equations.
Bred at a Scottish estate by crossing a flat-coated gun dog with Tweed Water Spaniels, this gentle, honey-coated working dog was recognized by the Kennel Club in 1913 — which breed?
Golden Retriever: Scottish breed of dog. It is characterised by a gentle and affectionate nature and a striking golden coat.
Published in 1931 by an Austrian logician, these two results proved that any consistent axiom system for arithmetic will always contain true statements it cannot prove — what are they called?
Gödel's incompleteness theorems: Limitative results in mathematical logic.

This French mathematician reinvented what it means to find the area under a curve, publishing his sweeping new theory of integration in a 1902 dissertation titled "Integral, length, area." Who was he?
Strongly associated with human habitation and now the most widely distributed wild bird on Earth thanks to introductions across multiple continents, this small brown-and-black bird is which species?
House sparrow: Species of bird. The house sparrow (Passer domesticus) is a bird of the sparrow family Passeridae, found in most parts of the world.

Once diagnosed almost exclusively in women during the 19th century and studied intensely by Sigmund Freud and Jean-Martin Charcot, this term for 'ungovernable emotional excess' is no longer accepted as a medical diagnosis. What is it called?
Hysteria: Excess, ungovernable emotion. Hysteria is a term used to mean ungovernable emotional excess and can refer to a temporary state of mind or emotion.

He won the 1944 Nobel Prize for his resonance method of recording the magnetic properties of atomic nuclei, and was among the first Americans to work on the cavity magnetron behind radar and microwave ovens — which physicist?

A former Chicago options trader with finance degrees but no PhD, this entrepreneur co-founded a dot-com company whose peer-reviewed project evolved into the world's largest free encyclopedia — who is he?

Caused by a herpesvirus and linked to weakened immunity such as HIV/AIDS, this cancer produces purple skin lesions and disproportionately affects older Mediterranean men in its 'classic' form — which condition?
Kaposi's sarcoma: Cancer of the skin, integumentary lymph nodes, or other organs.
About 1.5 metres long and beginning at the cecum via the ileocecal valve, this final section of the human gut absorbs water and salt before waste reaches the rectum — what part of the body is it?
Large intestine: Last part of the digestive system in vertebrates.
Sometimes called the paleomammalian cortex, this set of brain structures — including the amygdala — governs emotion, motivation, and long-term memory — what is it called?
Limbic system: Set of brain structures involved in emotion and motivation. Its various components support a variety of functions including emotion, behavior, long-term memory, and olfaction.

This German fluid dynamicist built the mathematical foundations of subsonic aerodynamics, identifying the 'boundary layer' and lifting-line theory — and lent his name to a dimensionless number. Who was he?

First isolated in the 1770s and carrying atomic number 25, this hard, silvery transition metal is a key alloying agent in stainless steel and also an essential trace nutrient in the human diet — which element?
Manganese: Chemical element with atomic number 25 (Mn)

First synthesized near Darmstadt in 1982, this fleeting synthetic element — its most stable isotope lasts mere seconds — was named for the Austrian-Swedish nuclear physicist Lise Meitner. Which element is it?
Meitnerium: Chemical element with atomic number 109 (Mt)
North of the Arctic Circle in summer, this phenomenon keeps the sky lit long after the clock strikes twelve — what is it called?
Midnight sun: Natural phenomenon when daylight lasts for a whole day.
This rounded mound of fatty tissue overlies the junction where the two pubic bones meet — what is it?
Mons pubis: Rounded mass of fatty tissue found over the pubic symphysis.

The first production helicopter with fully fly-by-wire flight controls, this European twin-engine military chopper comes in troop-transport and naval anti-submarine variants flown by over a dozen NATO nations. What is it?
NHIndustries NH90: Family of military helicopters.
Surrounded by a typically darker-colored areola, this raised region of breast tissue is where milk exits through the lactiferous ducts during lactation — what is it?
Nipple: Part of the breast. The milk can flow through the nipple passively, or it can be ejected by smooth muscle contractions that occur along with the ductal system.
A Boston physician, medical reformer, and 'fireside' poet, this polymath delighted readers with his 'Breakfast-Table' series begun in 1858. Who was he?
Oliver Wendell Holmes Sr.: American poet, essayist, physician (1809–1894)
With long dense grey fur and rounded ears set oddly low on the sides of its head, this small wild cat — first described in 1776 near Lake Baikal — roams the cold steppes of Central Asia. What is it?
Pallas's cat: Species of small wild cat. Pallas's cat (Otocolobus manul), also called manul, is a small wild cat with long and dense light grey fur, and rounded ears set low on the sides of the head.
Commonly called geraniums or storksbills, this genus of roughly 280 evergreen species was split from a related genus by a botanist in 1789 — which genus, native largely to southern Africa?
Pelargonium: Genus of plants. It includes about 280 species of perennials, succulents, and shrubs.

Nicknamed 'terror birds,' this family of large, mostly flightless carnivores roamed the Americas from the Cenozoic era, with one genus, Titanis, reaching as far as the southern United States — which family?
Phorusrhacidae: Extinct family of flightless birds. The exact number of genera is uncertain, as some taxa such as Brontornis may be different forms of bird instead.
Named after the American diplomat who introduced it from Mexico, this red-and-green Christmas plant is not actually toxic to pets — which plant?
Also known as face blindness, this cognitive disorder leaves a person unable to recognize familiar faces — even their own — while other visual skills stay intact. What is it?
Prosopagnosia: Cognitive disorder of face perception. Prosopagnosia should not be confused with prosopometamorphopsia, a disorder characterized by altered perceptions of faces.
Some specimens of this native European tree, whose acorns dangle on long stalks, are believed to be over 1,000 years old — name the species?
Quercus robur: Species of flowering plant.
Striking children recovering from a viral illness like the flu, this brain disease has been linked in about 90% of cases to aspirin use — what is it called?
Reye syndrome: Rapidly worsening brain disease.
Discovered in 1861 via flame spectroscopy by Bunsen and Kirchhoff, this alkali metal is named from the Latin word for 'deep red' — which element?
Rubidium: Chemical element with atomic number 37 (Rb)
Caused by the same Group A strep behind strep throat, this childhood illness brings a sandpapery red rash and a bumpy tongue — what is it?
An adult female of this ruminant is a ewe, a castrated male a wether, and a young one a lamb — and with about 1.2 billion of them, they're easily the most common of their kind. What animal?
Sheep: Domesticated ruminant bred for meat, wool, and milk.
With the formula Na2SO4, this white, water-soluble compound is produced at six million tonnes a year and used as a filler in powdered laundry detergent — which compound?

Sodium sulfate: Chemical compound with formula Na2SO4. Sodium sulfate (also known as sodium sulphate or sulfate of soda) is the inorganic compound with formula Na2SO4 as well as several related hydrates.

An English dyer and astronomer, he was the first to systematically show, around 1729, that electricity could travel through metals — flipping the era's focus from mere static sparks to conduction. Who was he?
Stephen Gray (scientist): English physicist. Stephen Gray (December 1666 – February 1736) was an English dyer and astronomer who was the first to systematically experiment with electrical conduction.
Derived from a Greek word meaning 'concurrence,' this medical term describes a set of signs and symptoms that tend to occur together — what is it called?
Syndrome: Association of several clinically recognizable features.
